entities.summary:
Caecilianus, Bishop of Carthage from approximately 311 CE until his death after 321 CE, was a pivotal figure in the early Christian Church whose contested election ignited the Donatist schism, a profound and enduring theological and political crisis in Roman North Africa. Active during the critical transition from imperial persecution to official tolerance under Constantine the Great, Caecilianus's legitimacy became the focal point for deeply rooted tensions within the African church, particularly concerning the readmission of those who had compromised their faith during the Diocletianic Persecution.

The core events surrounding Caecilianus's significance began with his election as Bishop of Carthage in 311 CE, following the death of Mensurius. His consecration was performed by Felix of Aptunga, a bishop accused by rivals of being a "traditor" – one who had surrendered sacred texts to Roman authorities during the persecutions. This accusation, combined with the fact that Caecilianus was consecrated without the presence of the senior Numidian bishops, fueled opposition. His detractors, led by the wealthy and influential matron Lucilla and eventually by Majorinus and Donatus, consecrated a rival bishop, Majorinus, initiating a parallel episcopate that escalated into a full-blown schism. Emperor Constantine, initially seeking to unify the church, summoned councils at Rome (313 CE) and Arles (314 CE) to adjudicate the dispute, both of which affirmed Caecilianus's legitimacy and the validity of his consecration.
